alt: A specification point has a requirement, a measurable target and a reason from research, plus a column for how it will be tested. Example: the planter must hold 6 kg with 5 mm or less deflection, because of three pots of wet soil plus a safety margin, tested with weights. A point like “It must be strong” has no target and cannot be tested.
caption: Requirement, measurable target and reason, plus a test that Criterion D will use.

after: ## Worked project used in this guide
alt: Front and side views of a planter on a balcony railing. Railing posts are 500 mm apart, so the planter holding three 90 mm pots is at most 450 mm long. In side view it clamps over a top rail 40 to 60 mm wide (measured at 48 mm) without drilling and projects no more than 180 mm.
caption: The client’s measured balcony sets the planter’s size and fixing limits.

after: ## 2. Generating a range of feasible ideas
alt: Three copies of the same trough in three colours count as one idea. A genuine range for the planter: idea A, a folded aluminium trough with hooks over the rail; idea B, an exterior-plywood shelf gripped by two screw clamps; idea C, recycled PET felt pockets hung from a strap.
caption: Ideas form a range only if they solve the problem in different ways.

after: ## 2. Generating a range of feasible ideas
alt: Four ways to generate ideas, annotated sketching, mind maps, morphological charts and SCAMPER, feed a funnel that checks each idea against skills, tools, materials, time and budget. The result is written into the annotation, for example noting that the school has a folding bar for sheet metal.
caption: An idea is feasible only if it can really be made with what is available.

alt: Stacked bars show each idea’s weighted points for seven specification criteria, with weights 3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1 and 1. Idea A totals 50, idea B 54 and idea C 43, out of a maximum of 65. Idea B’s working is 15 + 15 + 8 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 54.
caption: Weight times score, added up: B leads, but the total still needs a written justification.

alt: Five steps of a justification for the planter: state the choice and score (B, 54 of 65), name the specification points it meets, compare with the rejected ideas A and C, include the client’s feedback, and admit B’s weakness in weather resistance with a plan to use exterior varnish and stainless screws.
caption: A justification compares ideas against named specification points, then plans development.

after: ## 4. Presenting the solution: planning drawings and diagrams
alt: Two layouts of the same three views. In third-angle projection the plan sits above the front view and the right-hand end view sits to its right. In first-angle projection the plan sits below the front view and the view from the left sits to its right. Every drawing needs the projection symbol, a scale, key dimensions and a note that all dimensions are in mm.
caption: Where the plan sits tells you which projection method was used.

after: ## 4. Presenting the solution: planning drawings and diagrams
alt: Two A4 landscape sheets with a dashed 277 by 190 mm usable area. At 1:2 the front, plan and end views of the 450 by 180 by 120 mm planter need 335 mm of width and run off the sheet. At 1:5 they need 146 by 80 mm and fit, so a 90 mm pot hole is drawn 18 mm across.
caption: Work out the space the views need at each scale before you start drawing.
